readerTitle: Profitable, and still out of cash
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 도매업체, 인테리어 시공업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익은 사업이 돈을 버는지를 알려주고, 현금은 이번 달을 버틸 수 있는지를 알려준다. 둘은 서로 다른 시계로 움직인다.
misconception: 이익이 났으면 그만큼 통장에 돈이 늘어 있다. 이익을 내는 사업은 돈이 떨어질 일이 없다.

sources.text: 재무회계의 표준 개념 (발생주의 이익과 현금 흐름의 차이)

factChecks.note: "Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is reality"는 출처가 불분명한 업계 격언입니다. 카드에는 특정 인물에게 귀속하지 않고 "an old saying"으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Profitable, and still out of cash
body: Lena runs a small kitchenware distributor. In March she lands her biggest order ever and makes a profit.
At the end of the month, her bank account is overdrawn. Nothing went wrong. Nobody cheated her. The numbers just moved on two different clocks.

image.label: A profit report showing a gain next to a bank app showing a negative balance
image.brief: 창고 사무실 책상 위. 왼쪽에 초록색 "+$5,000"이 적힌 손익 보고서, 오른쪽에 빨간색 "−$15,000"이 뜬 휴대폰 은행 앱 화면. 뒤로 냄비·팬 상자가 쌓인 선반. 실제 은행·브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What does the bank show at the end of March?
body: Lena starts March with $40,000 in the bank. She sells $60,000 of goods to a chain of shops, which will pay in 60 days.
She pays her supplier $45,000 for those goods on delivery, plus $10,000 for staff and the warehouse. Her accountant reports a March profit of $5,000.

options.feedback: That would be true if every sale were paid the day it happened. Here the $60,000 hasn't arrived, but the costs have already left.

options.text: About $40,000: the profit is only on paper for now
options.feedback: Right that the profit isn't cash yet. But the money she paid out is very real, and it's already gone.
Yes. $55,000 went out and nothing came in. The profit is real, but it's sitting in a promise to pay, not in the bank.

cards.title: Same month, two stories.
body: In May the shops pay $60,000, and the balance jumps to $45,000: the starting $40,000 plus the $5,000 profit. The profit was right all along. It was just **two months early**.

breakdown.label: Cash out
breakdown.detail: Supplier and staff paid in March

cards.title: Profit vs cash
body: **Profit** counts a sale when you make it, and counts the costs that belong to that sale at the same time. It answers: did this work earn money?
**Cash** counts money only when it actually moves in or out of your account. It answers: can I pay what's due this week?
Both describe the same business. They just record events at different moments.

image.label: Two clocks: one marks when a sale is made, one marks when money moves
image.brief: 시계 두 개를 나란히 배치. 왼쪽 "Profit clock"은 3월에 바늘이 "Sale made"를 가리킴. 오른쪽 "Cash clock"은 5월에 "Money arrives"를 가리킴. 두 시계 사이에 "60 days"라고 적힌 점선 화살표.

cards.title: Where the two clocks drift apart.
body: The gap almost always comes from timing. A few common causes:
list: **Customers pay later:** profit now, cash later
**Stock bought ahead:** cash out now, cost counted only when it sells
**Equipment:** cash out at once, cost spread over years in profit
**Loan repayments:** cash out, but not a cost at all
**Customer deposits:** cash in now, profit only once the work is done
cards.callout: None of these are mistakes. They're just money and earnings arriving at different times.
cards.softwareNote: A software company selling annual plans paid upfront collects a year of cash on day one but earns the revenue month by month. Sell to large companies that pay 90 days after invoice, and the clocks flip the other way.

cards.title: Growth makes the gap bigger.
body: Say Lena's next order is twice as big. Profit doubles to $10,000. But she now has to pay out about $110,000 before a single dollar comes back.
The faster a business like this grows, the more cash it needs up front. That's how a company can be profitable, growing and still unable to pay its staff on Friday.
There's an old saying: *revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is reality.*

cards.title: Cash isn't the "real" number either.
body: Plenty of cash can hide a business that loses money. Customer deposits, unpaid supplier bills or a fresh loan all fill the account without earning anything.

A full bank account can feel like success while every job loses a little. Profit tells you whether the business works. Cash tells you whether it survives until the profit arrives. Watch both, and never treat one as proof of the other.

cards.title: Now it's a renovation contractor.
body: You're offered a $30,000 kitchen remodel. Materials cost $12,000 and crew wages $12,000, both paid during the six-week job. Profit: $6,000.
The client wants to pay everything on completion. You have $15,000 in the bank.

options.text: Take it as offered. It's clearly profitable
options.feedback: The profit is real, but you'd need $24,000 before getting paid and you have $15,000. You could run dry in week four.

options.text: Take it, but ask for 30% upfront, 40% halfway and 30% at the end
options.feedback: You keep the same $6,000 profit, but cash now arrives alongside costs. Your balance never drops below about $12,000.

options.text: Turn it down. The cash risk is too high
options.feedback: It protects your account, but you give up a good job. The problem is the timing of payment, and timing can often be negotiated.

cards.softwareNote: The same check applies to a software agency building a custom app: if the client pays on launch, your developers' salaries come out months before the money comes in.

cards.title: Profit says the business works. Cash says it makes it to Friday.
body: A profitable sale only helps you once the money arrives. Until then, you're paying for it.
**Try it today:** take your next big order or project. Write down, week by week, when money goes out and when it comes in. Find the lowest point in your bank balance.
